problem:
Find ${lim}_{t\to 1}[4f(t)-g(t)]$ given that $f(t)$ and $g(t)$ are defined as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t) & ={t}^{2}\,i+t\,j+\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,k \\ g(t) & =\frac{3}{t}\,i+(4-t)\,j-({t}^{2}-1)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Limit of a Sum of Vector Functions
examples.problem:
Find $\displaystyle \lim_{t \to 0} \big[ \mathbf f(t) - 2 \mathbf g(t) \big]$ given that $\mathbf f(t)$ and $\mathbf g(t)$ are defined as:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t)=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ {e}^{t} \\ t\end{aligned}],\,g(t)=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 1 \\ 2t\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$
examples.worked_solution:
First, we find the limit of each function:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 0}f(t)=[\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 0}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ {lim}_{t\to 0}{e}^{t} \\ {lim}_{t\to 0}t\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡0 \\ {e}^{0} \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ {lim}_{t\to 0}g(t)=[\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 0}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ {lim}_{t\to 0}1 \\ {lim}_{t\to 0}2t\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡0 \\ 1 \\ 2(0)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use properties of limits to calculate the final result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 0}[f(t)-2g(t)] & ={lim}_{t\to 0}f(t)-2{lim}_{t\to 0}g(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.worked_solution:
First, recall that

$$
{lim}_{t\to \pi }f(t)=[\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to \pi }\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\pi }{t} \\ {lim}_{t\to \pi }\frac{2t}{\pi } \\ {lim}_{t\to \pi }\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi -t)}{\pi -t}\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we find the limits one by one.

- For the first component, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to \pi }\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\pi }{t} & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi -\pi }{\pi } \\  & =\frac{0-\pi }{\pi } \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to \pi }\frac{2t}{\pi } & =\frac{2\pi }{\pi }=2.\end{aligned}
$$

- The third component can be found using L'Hopital's Rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to \pi }\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi -t)}{\pi -t} & ={lim}_{t\to \pi }\frac{{(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi -t))}^{′}}{(\pi -t)^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{t\to \pi }\frac{-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi -t)}{(-1)} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi -\pi )}{1} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡0 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, ${lim}_{t\to \pi }f(t)=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Finally, the limit of $‖f(t)‖$ as $t$ approaches $\pi $ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to \pi }‖f(t)‖ & =‖{lim}_{t\to \pi }f(t)‖ \\  & =‖[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]‖ \\  & =\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{6}.\end{aligned}
$$
